questions.title: Is DPO just supervised learning on preferred responses?
questions.question_body: The DPO paper states that the method uses "a simple binary cross entropy objective" and eliminates reinforcement learning. Given that binary cross-entropy is a standard supervised learning loss, how is DPO fundamentally different from just doing supervised fine-tuning on the preferred completions $y_w$? The loss in Equation 7 looks like a classification loss, but what exactly is being classified, and why isn't this just supervised learning?

questions.title: Why does the partition function $Z(x)$ cancel out in the DPO derivation?
questions.question_body: In the DPO derivation, Equation 5 expresses the reward as $r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)} + \beta \log Z(x)$, where $Z(x)$ is the partition function. The paper then says that when substituting this into the Bradley-Terry preference model, "the partition function cancels." I can see that $Z(x)$ depends only on $x$ and not on $y$, and the Bradley-Terry model depends on reward differences $r(x, y_1) - r(x, y_2)$. Is the cancellation simply because $\beta \log Z(x)$ appears in both terms and subtracts to zero? Are there any subtleties I'm missing in this algebraic step?

questions.title: What exactly is the 'implicit reward model' in DPO and how can a policy represent a reward?
questions.question_body: The paper defines an implicit reward as $\hat{r}_\theta(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$ and says "the policy network represents both the language model and the (implicit) reward." In standard RLHF, the reward model is a separate neural network that takes $(x, y)$ and outputs a scalar reward. In DPO, is the reward just defined as the log-ratio between the current policy and a reference policy? If so, how can this simple log-ratio be equivalent to a learned reward model that could have arbitrary complexity? What is the intuition for why this parameterization is sufficient?

questions.title: What does it mean for two reward functions to be in the same 'equivalence class' and why does it matter?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.1, the paper defines that two reward functions $r(x,y)$ and $r'(x,y)$ are equivalent if $r(x,y) - r'(x,y) = f(x)$ for some function $f$. Lemma 1 says such rewards induce the same preference distribution, and Lemma 2 says they induce the same optimal policy. Why does adding any function of $x$ alone not change preferences? And why is this equivalence relation important for the DPO derivation — does it mean we have freedom in how we parameterize the reward?

questions.title: What are the 'mild assumptions' in Theorem 1 and does it guarantee DPO can represent any reward?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states: "Under mild assumptions, all reward classes consistent with the Plackett-Luce (and Bradley-Terry in particular) models can be represented with the reparameterization $r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$." What exactly are these "mild assumptions"? The proof sketch mentions a projection operator $f$ that normalizes the reward, but I'm unclear on what conditions are needed for this to work. Does this theorem mean DPO can represent any possible reward function, or are there restrictions on what rewards can be learned?

questions.title: How does DPO avoid the instability issues of actor-critic algorithms like PPO?
questions.question_body: Section 5.2 discusses instability in PPO and mentions that the normalization term $f(r_\phi, \pi_{\text{ref}}, \beta)$ acts as a "soft value function" that, without it, causes high variance in policy gradients. The paper says "the DPO reparameterization yields a reward function that does not require any baselines." But I don't understand the connection: DPO never computes this normalization term, so how does it avoid the variance issue? Is it because DPO doesn't use policy gradients at all, or is there something about the reparameterization that inherently solves this problem?

questions.title: Why does the naive probability ratio approach cause model degeneration without the DPO weighting?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that a "naive probability ratio objective" without the weighting coefficient causes model degeneration (referencing Appendix Table 5). The DPO gradient includes an importance weight $\sigma(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w))$ that gives "higher weight when reward estimate is wrong." What exactly happens when this weight is removed? Does the model collapse, or does it just overfit? What is the mechanistic explanation for why the weighting prevents degeneration?

questions.title: Does DPO truly optimize the same objective as RLHF, or is there an approximation?
questions.question_body: The paper claims DPO "implicitly optimizes the same objective as existing RLHF algorithms (reward maximization with a KL-divergence constraint)." But DPO uses a completely different optimization procedure — a classification loss rather than reinforcement learning. Is the DPO objective mathematically equivalent to the RLHF objective in Equation 3, or is there some approximation being made? If they are truly equivalent, why does DPO achieve better empirical results than PPO in some experiments — shouldn't they converge to the same solution?

questions.title: Why do we need a separate frozen reference model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ throughout DPO training?
questions.question_body: The paper says $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is typically initialized as $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$, and the DPO loss (Equation 7) involves both $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Why can't we just use the current model $\pi_\theta$ as its own reference (i.e., set $\pi_{\text{ref}} = \pi_\theta$)? The reference model appears in the log-ratios in the loss — what would go wrong if it were the same as the model being trained? Also, the paper mentions initializing $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by fine-tuning on preferred completions when SFT is unavailable. Why is this particular initialization important?

questions.title: How should the $\beta$ parameter be chosen in DPO and what are the tradeoffs?
questions.question_body: The $\beta$ parameter controls the KL constraint strength. The paper uses values like $\beta \in \{0.05, 0.1, 1, 5\}$ in the sentiment experiments and says they "did not meaningfully tune DPO's $\beta$ hyperparameter" for summarization. What are the tradeoffs in choosing $\beta$? Does a higher $\beta$ mean the model stays closer to the reference policy (more conservative) or farther from it? Is there a principled way to set this value, or is it purely empirical? Also, how does $\beta$ relate to the KL constraint in the original RLHF objective (Equation 3)?

questions.title: What happens if human preferences don't actually follow the Bradley-Terry model?
questions.question_body: DPO assumes preferences follow the Bradley-Terry model where $p^*(y_1 \succ y_2 | x) = \sigma(r^*(x, y_1) - r^*(x, y_2))$. But what if real human preferences are more complex — for example, intransitive (where A is preferred to B, B to C, but C to A), or dependent on factors not captured by a single scalar reward? The paper mentions Plackett-Luce models as a generalization, but this still assumes a scalar reward ranking. Would DPO still produce a meaningful policy if preferences violate these assumptions, and how would we detect this problem?

questions.title: How is the reward-KL frontier used to compare DPO and PPO in the sentiment experiments?
questions.question_body: In the controlled sentiment generation experiment, the paper evaluates algorithms by their "frontier of achieved reward and KL-divergence from the reference policy." I understand that higher reward and lower KL are both desirable, but how exactly is this frontier computed and compared? The paper runs experiments with different hyperparameters ($\beta$ for DPO, target KL for PPO) and plots reward vs. KL. Is the comparison based on Pareto dominance, or is there a specific metric? Also, what does it mean that "DPO's reward/KL tradeoff strictly dominates PPO" — does this mean DPO is better at every point on the frontier?
